1245-night-and-day:
Virginia Woolf's second novel follows Katharine Hilbery, a young woman of a literary London family, torn between a safe marriage to a poet and her love for Ralph Denham, a struggling solicitor. The tale moves through drawing rooms, offices, and walks along the Thames.

Woolf writes London life with care and wit, and the novel's question is modern: can a woman have both love and a life of her own? The book, more traditional than her later work, still shows her eye for the inner life. It draws readers who like Woolf before the experiments.
1336-shelley-an-essay:
Written from a Catholic point of view, this short essay takes up the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley and asks why the Church had let poetry slip from its care. It argues that song and faith once grew side by side, in Dante and in Francis of Assisi, and that casting poetry out harmed both faith and art.

The writer then reads Shelley as a poet of beauty who reached toward light through nature and love, even while standing outside the Church. The essay pleads for poets to be welcomed back as helpers of the mind. It is less a life of Shelley than a case for poetry as a spiritual art.
1755-ivanoff-a-play:
Nicholas Ivanoff is a landowner worn down by debt, a dying wife, and his own loss of purpose, and he cannot explain his coldness even to himself. Anna, born Sarah Abramson, loves him still, while his uncle Count Shabelski and his neighbor Lebedieff press him toward a new match with Lebedieff's daughter.

The play's tension is inward: Ivanoff cannot explain his own coldness, and his honesty makes him crueller than a villain would be. Chekhov wrote it as a study of a man out of step with his age. It remains a sharp portrait of depression before the word was common, played out in drawing rooms and country houses.
1759-the-black-bearded-barbarian-the-lif:
Mary Esther Miller MacGregor, writing as Marion Keith, tells the life of George Leslie Mackay, the Canadian missionary whom the Chinese of north Formosa called the Black-Bearded Barbarian. The book opens with Mackay as a boy splitting rocks in a stony pasture behind the barn. It follows him to Formosa, where he preached nearly every day in houses by the river and in open squares.

Mackay also treated disease wherever he found it, and the biography stresses his plain manner and his stamina. Written for young readers, it presents a missionary life as adventure and service together, and it keeps its focus on the man himself rather than on doctrine.
1820-a-wasted-day:
Richard Harding Davis opens with a private secretary laying a letter in front of the Wisest Man in Wall Street, a note from Mrs. Austin, probation officer of the Court of General Sessions, asking for a letter about a young man named Spear. The wise man, Mr. Thorndike, must decide whether a word from him can save a boy from prison.

The story follows Thorndike through a day of meetings, with Mr. Andrews explaining from the depth of his wisdom that mothers are all alike when a son goes to jail. Davis uses the day to ask what wisdom is worth if it cannot act. The tale ends as a quiet rebuke to men who are wise about markets and helpless about mercy.
1878-a-millionaire-of-yesterday:
'Filth. ' grunts Trent at a cabin in the west of Ireland, and the novel that follows moves from such places into finance, diamonds, and South African mines. Da Souza, with beady eyes, brings news that stuns a roomful of men. The millionaire of the title must reckon with a past that will not stay buried.

Oppenheim writes the Edwardian thriller of wealth with confidence, and the novel's interest lies in its hero's rise and the price of it. Readers who like stories of fortunes made fast and lost faster will find the book brisk, worldly, and full of the author's usual polish.
1932-early-kings-of-norway:
Thomas Carlyle's Early Kings of Norway, taken from volume nineteen of the Sterling Edition of his works, tells the saga age in Carlyle's thunderous prose. Olaf, baptized but still a viking, keeps his profession, and his partnerships with Svein of the Double-beard carry him through raids and conversions.

Carlyle treats the Norse kings as heroes of a stern age, and his chapters mix saga narrative with moral commentary. The book is less a modern history than a Victorian retelling. Its value lies in Carlyle's voice: a prophet-historian who believed that great men, for good or ill, make the ages they live in.
20074-the-story-of-the-cambrian-a-biogra:
C. P. Gasquoine wrote The Story of the Cambrian, a biography of a railway in Wales. Railways rarely get life stories, yet the Cambrian lines had a long, hard one. Gasquoine thanks many friends tied to the Cambrian Railways for their help. Their aid made even an attempt at the tale possible, he says.

Inside are lines, stations, firms, and the men who ran them. Welsh hills and coastal towns shaped every mile of track. The book records growth, strain, and change in one rail system. Readers who love rail history get names, dates, and local detail in depth.
20164-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote Critical Miscellanies, and volume one holds an essay on Macaulay. Morley was a leading critic and statesman of Victorian Britain. He praises the habit of writing down what one reads and thinks. Such notes give learning clearness, shape, and a right place, he says.

Macaulay, the famed historian and essayist, is a fit subject for Morley. Both men wrote prose of great force and wide public reach. The essay weighs Macaulay's gifts, faults, and place in English letters. Readers get two sharp Victorian minds meeting on the page at once.
20201-mary-gray:
Mary Gray is a novel of a girl raised in a poor London street. Her home was one of a squat line of mean little houses. Those houses hid behind a great church in the city's heart. The road before them led only to the church's back entrance.

From such narrow ground, Mary Gray's life and choices unfold. Poverty, work, and love test girls in tales of this kind. The church at her back stands as both shelter and shadow. Readers get a sober city novel on a poor girl's path to womanhood.
20575-my-dog-tray:
My Dog Tray is a story in verse and prose for children, about a poor girl named Nelly and her faithful dog. Tray never leaves her side. At night, while Nelly's tears are shed in hushed sorrow, the dog crouches close to keep her warm.

With pitying love, Tray licks her bitter tears away. Nelly shares her crusts with him, and he shares her hard life with a dog's steady heart. Tales like this one, of animal faithfulness to a suffering child, were nursery favorites in the Victorian years. Tray's devotion carries the whole lesson of the book.
20736-the-girl-scouts-at-home-or-rosanna:
Katherine Keene Galt wrote Rosanna's Beautiful Day for the Girl Scouts at Home set of tales. One scene shows a big garage, fit for four cars, wrapped in vines. Its one door opens into a garden, with no other door or window on that side.

Rosanna's day turns small home events into a full, happy arc for young readers. Scouting values of help, cheer, and care run through the tale. The book shows how early Scout fiction brought the movement into ordinary homes. It keeps a light touch, with family scenes and outdoor touches in equal share.
21116-the-easiest-way:
Eugene Walter's play The Easiest Way became this 1911 novel, written with Arthur Hornblow as a story of metropolitan life. Its heroine, Laura Murdock, calls herself an actress, though the foreword insists she has no talent for the stage. She has lived as a kept woman and wants to change.

Laura tries to redeem her past through an honest, unselfish love. The attempt fails badly, and she falls back toward the easy way of the title. The authors stress that working actors should not be judged by Laura's type. Broadway crowds and New York rooms frame her rise and collapse.
21228-white-lilac-or-the-queen-of-the-ma:
Amy Walton's story for girls begins with Mrs White at her cottage door. She is anxious about a promised visit from the rector's wife to see the new baby. Several of her children have died, so this one matters all the more. A branch of white lilac, brought by her husband, gives the baby her name: Lilac White.

Her father dies soon after, and her mother raises her alone. At twelve Lilac is pretty enough for a visiting artist to want her in a picture, until a cousin's new hair-do spoils the sitting. May Day brings rivalry over Queen of the May, and grief follows close behind the honour.
21267-lincoln-s-birthday:
Robert Haven Schauffler edited this anthology for the Our American Holidays series, published in New York in 1909 and reprinted through 1916. It promises a full view of Lincoln through the most noteworthy essays, orations, and poems about him, plus fiction and Lincoln's own writings. Thanksgiving and Christmas volumes stand beside it in the series.

Schools and families used such anthologies to mark February 12 with readings rather than only ceremony. Pieces from many ages and nations show Lincoln as others saw him: speaker, president, and folk hero. The editor thanks many publishers for permissions. It is a period piece of Lincoln devotion, gathered for one day a year.
2140-extracts-from-the-diary-of-william-:
William Bray, born at Shere in 1736, kept a diary from 1756 to 1800, and these extracts, printed in 1876 for his descendants, show a life of sociability, amusement, and successful industry. His brothers died unmarried, and he succeeded to the family estate in 1803. Bray's diary, kept for decades, shows a gentleman's round of visits, dinners, and business.

The diary records dinners, visits, business, and local life with steady good humour. Readers of Georgian social history will find here an ordinary gentleman's round, told without pretence and full of small, telling detail. The 1876 printing, made for family, now serves historians of Georgian sociability.
21758-hudson-bay:
In May 1841, a letter changed young R. M. Ballantyne's life: he was appointed apprentice clerk to the Hudson's Bay Company. This book is his own account of the years that followed, in the fur country of Canada. In his preface he says his chief aim is the everyday life of that world, a subject other writers had only touched in passing.

The pages follow the daily work of the trade: the outposts, the Red River Settlement, the travel, and the long winters. Later editions kept the text nearly as written, since the far posts changed so slowly. Every novel Ballantyne later wrote about the north grew from these years. As memoir, it is the seed of them all.
21782-the-yillian-way:
Jame Retief, vice-consul in Earth's Diplomatic Corps, faces the most polite danger in the galaxy in Keith Laumer's The Yillian Way. The Yill of the title are gray-skinned hosts whose ceremonial protocol is impressive, colorful, and, in the long run, deadly. Retief watches a Yill party where a raised fist and hands on a head pass for friendly custom. Every gesture means something, and a wrong one could kill.

The ambassador's staff insists that Terrestrials are a kindly, peace-loving race. Retief, junior and sharp-eyed, must work the mission in harmony while the Yill smile and sip lavender drinks. Laumer builds the tale on manners as warfare. It is a sly, funny story of diplomacy where etiquette itself is the trap.
21836-the-tale-of-jasper-jay:
Jasper Jay, the noisiest rogue in Pleasant Valley, stars in this 1917 children's tale by Arthur Scott Bailey. Some birds called old Mr. Crow the loudest in the neighborhood, but they had forgotten his knavish cousin. Jasper's shrieks ring over Farmer Green's pines on the coldest mornings, for he winters right there. He is bold and handsome in his bright blue suit, and a rogue for all that.

Chapters follow his jokes, boasts, and narrow escapes: scaring the hens, hiding from Solomon Owl, and joining the singing society. Bailey's Tuck-Me-In Tales teach nature through animal mischief. Jasper has to be got rid of more than once, and never quite is. Small readers learn the blue jay by laughing at him.
21846-crowded-out-o-crofield-or-the-boy-:
Jack Ogden, a blacksmith's boy in the village of Crofield, is crowded out into the wide world in this boys' novel by William O. Stoddard. Stoddard insists the tale is close to history: a real energetic boy was pushed from his village into a surprising career. Jack stands fifteen, sandy-haired and freckled, in the wide door of the smithy, looking toward the rickety bridge.

His road runs down the Hudson by steamboat, past the state-house, into the city and a new world. Chapters bring a runaway, a burglary charge, hunger, and work at all trades before complete success. Mary, the girl of the tale, sails her own course in the Eagle. It is a cheerful American success story of the old school.
22141-joy-in-service-forgetting-and-pres:
Joy in Service, issued by the American Tract Society in 1900, is a devotional book about the Christian life. Its full title runs Forgetting and Pressing Onward Until the Day Dawn. The writer argues that knowing Christ in history is not enough. A believer may admire Christ's power and adore him as Saviour, yet still long for a closer, personal acquaintance with him.

The chapters press readers toward active service done with joy. Forgetting what lies behind, they are to strain forward like Paul. Tract Society books were cheap, earnest, and everywhere in Protestant America. This one survives as a fair sample of the devotional reading that shaped ordinary churchgoers in 1900.
22267-a-woman-for-mayor-a-novel-of-to-da:
Helen M. Winslow, once editor of The Club Woman, wrote A Woman for Mayor as a novel of to-day in 1909. Her city, the talk runs, is going to the dogs. Municipal affairs were never so muddled, everybody agrees. Barnaby Burke is running for mayor with a ravenous pack of demagogues behind him, and honest citizens despair of the result.

Against Burke the reformers set a woman candidate. Winslow, who knew clubwomen and suffrage circles from inside, builds her plot on ward politics, newspapers, and drawing-room pressure. The question is whether a woman can clean a city hall. The novel is a suffrage argument wearing a story's clothes, lively and pointed.
22271-schwartz-a-history-from-schwartz-b:
Schwartz: A History is the title novel of David Christie Murray's linked volume Schwartz. Its narrator opens with a startling sentence: he was expatriated by a man with an axe. The man and the axe alike were visionary and unreal, he admits. Yet it took a strong effort of will to hold them at arm's length. Work on hand, and a mind broken down by overwork, explain the vision.

Murray builds the history out of that haunted start. Business, exile, and a disordered conscience drive Schwartz's story. The linked tales that follow share his world of Castle Barfield and London counting-houses. This opening piece shows Murray blending the ghostly with the commercial.
22273-bulldog-and-butterfly-from-schwart:
Bulldog and Butterfly, from David Christie Murray's Schwartz, opens with a map in words. Castle Barfield, Heydon Hey, and Beacon Hargate form three points of a triangle. Barfield has pretensions; Heydon Hey is a village; Beacon Hargate is no more than a hamlet. The house at the story's centre is crossed by great beams of black-painted oak, with diamond-paned windows sunk low in the walls.

Roses and honeysuckle cover the porch in summer, and the garden runs up to the house all round. Murray sets his contrast of bulldog and butterfly in this old place. Character against character, as the title promises, drives the slight tale. The Schwartz stories share this countryside.
22417-the-etiquette-of-to-day:
The Etiquette of To-Day, revised and enlarged in 1918, teaches the manners of its moment. It opens by naming the secret of success in society. That secret, it says, is heartiness and sympathy in company.

A man unhappy in company finds no fitting word ready. All his information sounds a little impertinent to others. A happy man finds lucky occasions at every turn. He introduces what he has to say with ease. The book builds its rules on that warm foundation. Calls, letters, dress, and table conduct follow in order. Readers get Edwardian-era social rules, useful now as a mirror of their world.
22720-the-minister-of-evil-the-secret-hi:
The Minister of Evil, subtitled The Secret History of Rasputin's Betrayal of Russia, is a 1917 insider's account of the fall of the Russian monarchy. The catalog record names no author. Its writer claims no literary renown and no pretence to fine phrases or elegant diplomacy.

The object, the author states plainly, is simply to set down the truth about Russia's crumbling and the fall of its throne. Rasputin, the Siberian holy man whose influence over the tsarina scandalized Russia, stands at the center as the minister of evil. Such books poured out in revolution's first year, mixing memoir, accusation, and grief. This one preserves the voice of a loyalist watching an empire dissolve.
2274-how-to-live-on-24-hours-a-day:
Arnold Bennett's brisk little book argues that the working day leaves everyone a hidden fortune: the hours before and after office work. How to Live on 24 Hours a Day urges clerks and office workers to claim ninety minutes each evening for reading, music, and self-improvement. That time should not slip away in tired routine. Bennett writes with cheerful bluntness.

His advice is practical rather than mystical: rise a little earlier, guard one evening, and treat the mind as a garden needing daily care. The book's fame comes from its plain arithmetic of time. Modern readers still find its message bracing and easy to try.
22758-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The New England Magazine presents its second number, volume 1, number 2, dated February 1886. The catalog record names no editor. A new regional magazine had to prove itself monthly, and this issue again mixes college history, essays, and literature for New England readers.

The sample article traces the founding impulse of Tufts College to a single sermon. Hosea Ballou the younger preached it before the General Convention of Universalists. The place was New York, in September 1847. From a sermon to a college is the kind of story the magazine loved: faith, education, and regional ambition in one thread. Poetry and fiction fill out the number. Together with its first issue, it shows the Bay State Monthly settling into the long career ahead of it.
22913-winning-his-way:
Charles Carleton Coffin's Winning His Way follows travelers into a beautiful valley. After weeks on dusty roads they reach a winding river, fair sunny hills, and groves of oak, maple, and linden. The air smells of honeysuckle and jasmine, and deer browse the tender grass on the slopes.

Coffin wrote history and adventure for boys, and this tale mixes settlement, striving, and scenery. A young hero makes his path in a new country, learning work and character along the way. The valley scene shows Coffin's method, rewarding effort with a rich land honestly described. His books taught generations of readers their American past. This one keeps the same earnest, outdoors spirit.
23024-grimm-tales-made-gay:
Guy Wetmore Carryl retells the Grimms in verse in Grimm Tales Made Gay. One tale turns on a will. Four-year-old Paul stands to take half the gold, while Beatrix, six, inherits the remainder. Uncle Ben responds with an act everyone calls splendid.

Carryl's trick is to keep the fairy-tale skeleton and swap the moral for a wink. His rhymes bounce, his endings swerve, and his morals arrive upside down on purpose. The book belonged to a brief vogue for comic retellings around 1900. Children can follow the stories, adults catch the jokes aimed over their heads. It remains a neat sample of light verse at its most professional.
23086-auction-of-to-day:
Milton C. Work calls the bids in Auction of To-Day, his 1913 guide to auction bridge. Work starts from a simple position, one spade opened and second hand passing. Case follows case from there. Dealer strength, raises to two and three spades, and minor-suit openings each get their treatment.

Work was America's bridge authority, and this book taught a generation how to bid the new auction game. Hands, conventions, and probabilities fill its pages in place of plot. Card historians prize such manuals, since they fix the exact moment when contract bridge was still unborn and auction ruled the clubs. Casual readers will find a vanished social world, conducted in spades.
23207-americans-all-stories-of-american-:
Americans All, from 1910, presents stories of American life of its own day. Its pages open by praising school days as days rich in experience. The first day at school, whether a little red schoolhouse or a big brick building holding a thousand pupils, is called the start of a new life.

As a model of school fiction, the book points to Emmy Lou, by George Madden Martin. That story follows a winsome girl from first grade through the end of high school. Readers get period stories and sketches that treat ordinary American childhood, school, and home life as worthy subjects.
2751-man-in-the-iron-mask-an-essay:
For nearly a hundred years the masked prisoner puzzled France, and this Dumas essay from Celebrated Crimes takes up the mystery. For nearly one hundred years, he notes, the masked prisoner's identity has puzzled France and tempted theorists.

Candidates parade past, twin brother, disgraced minister, royal bastard, and others, each tested against scant records. The essay is a piece of historical detective work, written with curiosity and flair. Readers get both a mystery and a lesson in how legends grow around a locked door. Dumas leaves the reader to judge which candidate fits best.
2916-the-foundations-an-extravagant-play:
John Galsworthy called The Foundations an extravagant play, setting its action continuously between eight and half past ten on a summer evening some years after the Great War. Lord William Dromondy, member of Parliament, keeps a Park Lane mansion whose cellar opens the play, while old Mrs. Lemmy's room in Bethnal Green gives the other pole. Anti-sweaters, sweated workers, a duke, and a crowd fill the cast.

The play contrasts rich and poor London directly, as little Aida runs in singing and chattering about a coffin followed to Hyde Park, better than a horse-drawn hearse. Galsworthy uses farce and satire to press a serious point about sweated labor. The Foundations shows his most experimental stage manner, broad in comedy and pointed in its social aim.
3178-the-gilded-age-a-tale-of-today:
Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote this 1873 novel together, and it gave an age its name. Squire Hawkins and his Tennessee land open the story, as he decides to remove to Missouri. He meets and adopts the boy Clay, survives a steamboat explosion, and takes in the little girl Laura. Colonel Beriah Sellers, dreamer of fortunes, joins the family circle.

Trouble and darkness follow, with a proposed sale of the Tennessee land hanging over all. The novel satirizes speculation, railroads, and Washington jobbery, where everything glitters and little is gold. Gilded, not golden, became the verdict on the era. The book remains the classic portrait of American greed dressed up as progress.
3244-to-him-that-hath-a-tale-of-the-west:
Ralph Connor titles this western novel from a Gospel line: to him that hath shall be given. The game opens it, with tennis calls of forty-love, game, and set. The cost of sacrifice, a heathen quest, and Annette follow, with the rectory and a grievance committee. A foreman, free speech, and the day before lead toward the night of victory.

A new manager, light that is darkness, and a strike carry the story into gathering clouds and a storm. A gallant fight closes the arc. Connor writes of labor, capital, and conscience in a mining west, where a manager's choices decide livelihoods. The novel argues, through its plot, that power used well grows and power hoarded fails.
3258-a-laodicean-a-story-of-to-day:
Thomas Hardy builds this novel around Paula, heiress of Stancy Castle, and the men who seek her. George Somerset, an architect, leads the first book, with Dare and Havill in the second. De Stancy takes the third, and the later books mix Somerset, Dare, and De Stancy around Paula herself. The preface notes how the old order of country manors may change slowly or suddenly.

Paula is a Laodicean in love and faith alike: warm to nothing fully, torn between modern ideas and old loyalties. Castle restoration becomes the novel's image for that divided mind, as new work meets old stone. Readers who like Hardy with a lighter touch will enjoy it, though the ending still carries his familiar irony about choices made too late.
3264-dennison-grant-a-novel-of-to-day:
Robert Stead sets this prairie novel in motion with a harvest shout. Chuck at the Y D tonight, and a bed under the shingles, Transley calls to the procession. Linder, foreman and head teamster, straightens from a half load of new hay, tightens the lines, and makes a sound in his throat. Horses press into their collars, and each wagon takes up its place.

Dennison Grant himself stands at the center of the farming world that follows. Stead, a Canadian novelist of the wheat lands, writes work as it was done: teams, hay, and weather deciding the day. A man's standing, earned in the field rather than declared in the town, is Stead's prairie measure throughout.
3468-poems-by-the-way:
William Morris gathers lyrics and short narrative poems in this collection, first printed in December 1891 and reprinted in 1892. Contents include From the Upland to the Sea, Of the Wooing of Hallbiorn the Strong, Echoes of Love's House, The Burghers' Battle, and The Hall and the Wood. The poems move between meadows, sea coasts, old halls, and the world of Norse legend.

Morris writes in a musical, old fashioned style, full of flowers, winds, and quiet longing. His speakers wander among bays and meads, sit in porches, and dream of a sun god's lonely home on a hill. The collection suits readers who enjoy late Victorian verse that looks back to medieval craft and story, rather than to city life.
3535-a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-bo:
Watkin Tench, a marine officer, writes a first hand account of the First Fleet voyage that founded the settlement at Botany Bay in Australia. Tench promises to keep the nautical detail brief, for the sake of general readers, and to offer both amusement and information. The expedition had excited wide curiosity in Britain, with hopes and fears about what a penal colony might become.

Tench describes the voyage, the landing, and the first encounters with the new land and its peoples. His little tract became one of the earliest published accounts of Australia. Readers interested in exploration, convict history, and the start of Sydney will find a clear, lively eyewitness narrative.
3702-foul-play:
Charles Reade and Dion Boucicault write a sensation novel that opens in a London merchant's dining room in Russell Square. The room is large, with sickly green walls, heavy maroon curtains, and mahogany chairs. A turkey carpet an inch thick covers the floor, in a place that seems at first sight inaccessible to romance. A young clerk, at school till fifteen and in his father's office till twenty two, shows such aptitude that the merchant John Wardlaw plans to advance him.

From this staid beginning the story moves into crime, forgery, shipwreck, and adventure, as Reade and Boucicault pile twists upon twists. The novel suits readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction at its most melodramatic, where a respectable office hides a plot that will carry its hero across the world.
3780-the-king-s-highway:
George Payne Rainsford James wrote this historical romance around a lover who dares to hope above his station. The hero loves a duke's daughter. Yet he knows the duke is proud of family, wealth, rank, and daughter alike. The duke has already favored a match with the son of the Earl of Byerdale, a nobleman of vast influence near the sovereign's counsels. The lover's suit must therefore fight pride, power, and an arranged rival.

James fills the tale with courts, country houses, and the codes of an older England, where a duke's consent counts as a great condescension. The prose is full and formal, in the manner of the early historical novel. Readers who enjoy Scott style romance will find a story of love against rank, told with ceremony and suspense.
3827-the-days-before-yesterday:
Lord Frederick Hamilton, encouraged by the welcome for his earlier reminiscences, offers a second lumber room of memories in this volume. He warns that readers hoping for scandals will be disappointed, since the book holds everyday events rather than revelations. Chapters recall a childhood of crocodiles, grizzlies, and chimney sweeps, a live lion at a tea party, and Landseer the painter as a family friend.

Later pages visit Paris, where judges dine and a Frenchman named Ducros cries Slop basin as his one word of English praise for a fine dish. Disraeli, Lord John Russell, and the Earl of Aberdeen pass through the narrative. Readers who like Victorian high society recalled without malice will find a genial and well mannered memoir.
4044-what-the-animals-do-and-say:
A natural history book for young readers gathers stories of what animals do and say, from farmyards to far islands. A writer on the Faroe Islands describes crow courts, where crows gather as if summoned, some with drooping heads and others grave as judges.

If a crow is proved guilty, the flock deals with it, in a folk tale of animal justice. Other chapters follow beasts, birds, and fishes through habits that seem almost human. The book suits children curious about nature, offering short, vivid tales that mix fact, fancy, and old country lore.
4078-the-picture-of-dorian-gray:
Oscar Wilde's novel follows Dorian Gray, a beautiful young man whose portrait ages while he stays young. In a sampled chapter, Dorian reclines in Lord Henry's little library in Curzon Street, among olive-stained oak, cream friezes, and silk Persian rugs.

Lord Henry's witty, corrupting talk shapes Dorian's path, as beauty, pleasure, and sin trade places in his life. Wilde writes with epigrams and rich description, turning a Faustian bargain into a study of art and morals. Readers who enjoy brilliant, unsettling fiction will find a short classic that still provokes debate.
5090-i-will-repay:
Baroness Orczy's novel opens in Paris in 1783, when a boy is publicly humiliated and swears revenge on the man who shamed him. Years later, in the shadow of the French Revolution, that oath returns to shape the lives of both men, as old debts, honour, and love collide amid political terror.

Orczy, best known for tales of the Revolution, writes a story of vengeance pursued to its bitter end. Disguises, narrow escapes, and moral choices test her characters. Readers get a romantic historical adventure in which a childhood vow proves harder to keep, and harder to escape, than either man expected.
515-margret-howth-a-story-of-to-day:
Rebecca Harding Davis sets this Civil War-era novel in a mill town shadowed by battle. Margret Howth, a teacher's daughter, faces work, poverty, and a lover torn between duty and doubt. Davis opens by refusing grand war themes, choosing instead homely, narrow life on the border of the battlefield.

Margret's story tracks mills, schools, and sickrooms, where plain folk bear grief in silence. Davis writes with moral gravity, seeking hope in humble things. The novel stands as an early realist portrait of wartime home life, where the true world grows, slowly, from endurance.
5229-felix-o-day:
F. Hopkinson Smith's novel Felix O'Day opens on Broadway, the Great White Way, where coloured signs pencil the skyline in fire and rain turns the asphalt to liquid gold. Through that crowded thoroughfare moves Felix, an Irish-American figure of the New York theatre and street world, whose fortunes the novel follows.

Smith writes with affection for old New York, its crowds, its traffic, and its sudden poetry. The book offers a warm, episodic portrait of city life in the early twentieth century, told by a writer who loved Broadway and knew its people from the inside.
5257-the-broad-highway:
Jeffery Farnol's Broad Highway opens with its narrator eating fried bacon with a tinker on a summer morning, dreaming of a book about roads, by-roads, wayside inns, and country people. The story itself begins with an uncle's will, then sends the hero out on foot, where he meets a bagman, a pugilist named Tom Cragg, a one-legged soldier, and many others.

Farnol writes a rambling, cheerful romance of the English road, in the manner of old picaresque tales. Readers will find inns, fights, love affairs, and landscape in generous measure. It is told by a narrator who loves the highway and the company found upon it.
5629-dorothy-dale-a-girl-of-to-day:
Margaret Penrose wrote Dorothy Dale: A Girl of To-Day as the first book of the Dorothy Dale series, followed by Dorothy Dale at Glenwood School. Contents run from Dorothy herself and Dorothy at the office through a strange adventure, a clew, and Miles Burlock. A swing, what happened in the orchard, Squire Sanders at school, apple blossom magic, and a soldier's daughter follow.

Later chapters bring an unprovoked attack, a queer picnic, a secret, Dorothy in politics, Dorothy in danger, a surprise trip, and an eventful journey. Penrose writes a modern girl's school and home adventures with warmth. Young readers get a cheerful series opener, full of friends, mysteries, and pluck.
5632-five-little-peppers-midway:
Margaret Sidney wrote Five Little Peppers Midway as another book about the Pepper family, lovingly inscribed to her little Margaret, who is Phronsie Pepper to all who know her. Contents run from Phronsie's Pie and Cousin Eunice Chatterton through rehearsals, welcome home, the little brown house, and old times again, to Badgertown calls, a sudden blow, and the party separating.

Poor Polly, new work for Polly, Mamsie's wedding, and questions of where Phronsie is and whether she is well again carry the family story forward. Readers get a warm, old-fashioned family tale, full of pies, plays, and Pepper loyalty.
5673-the-young-musician-or-fighting-his-:
Horatio Alger's novel follows Philip, a poor boy with a fiddle, who faces the threat of the poorhouse and a set of neighbors allied against him. The chapter titles trace his path. A call from Nick Holden comes first, then an auction and a fuss about his fiddle. A stay in the poorhouse and bad tidings follow, until he escapes on a night adventure. Music is both his gift and his trouble, since it marks him out and gives him a way forward.

We meet a classic Alger hero: young, hardworking, and determined to earn an honest living rather than accept charity or defeat. The story moves through small-town scheming, kindness from unexpected friends, and the slow turn of fortune that rewards persistence. It is a plain, encouraging tale for young readers, and a clear example of Alger's belief that pluck and honest work can change a life.
5698-fanny-s-first-play:
Bernard Shaw's Fanny's First Play, first published in 1911, is a comedy that turns the theatre itself into its subject. A young woman writes a play, and her family and their friends gather to judge it, bringing their own pride, prejudice, and respectability into the stalls with them. Shaw uses the occasion to mock critics, parents, and polite society in turn, letting each voice expose itself.

The fun comes from the layers: a play within a play, and an audience on stage watching an audience. Readers meet sharp dialogue, brisk reversals, and Shaw's familiar habit of letting a clever character say the uncomfortable truth aloud. It is a lively entry point to Shaw's stagecraft, and it still amuses readers who enjoy argument dressed up as entertainment.
5893-two-little-women-on-a-holiday:
Two Little Women on a Holiday follows two girls through a holiday of plans, arrivals, and small social adventures. Chapters trace a wonderful plan, a favourable decision, the arrival, a merry quartette, going about, a matinee idol, and great preparations. A caller, fine feathers, a skating party, collections, a lost jewel, suspicions, a tea room, and Dolly's ride carry the holiday forward.

Here is a bright girls' story of friendship, shopping, theatre, and mild mystery, where a lost jewel tests trust. The tone is cheerful and orderly, with holiday freedom balanced by good manners. Young readers who enjoy series stories of girls on holiday will find familiar pleasures here, and adults will enjoy its light, old-fashioned picture of leisure.
5894-the-extra-day:
Blackwood's The Extra Day follows children into a world where wonder interrupts ordinary time. Chapters trace the material and fancy as the seed of wonder. They move through the death of a mere fact and fact edged with fancy. Then come the birth and growth of wonder, before imagination wakes and wonder hides. A priest of wonder, fact and wonder in clash, and Judy's and Tim's particular adventures follow, as time hesitates and Maria stirs.

The book gives a children's fantasy of philosophy, where a day outside time lets young heroes see the world afresh. Blackwood writes with lyric feeling, favoring mood and image over plot machinery. The book suits readers of classic children's fantasy, and adults who enjoy stories where wonder itself is the adventure, granted for one extra day.
598-heimskringla-or-the-chronicle-of-the:
Snorri Sturluson chronicles Norway's kings from about 850 to 1177 in this saga collection, written in Old Norse around 1225. Sixteen sagas run from Halfdan the Black and Harald Fairhair through Olaf Trygvason, Saint Olaf, Harald Hardrada, and Magnus Barefoot to later kings. Family trees, songs, and old tales ground the history.

Sturluson writes as poet and historian, mixing fact with legend in clear, stark prose. Scholars debate his accuracy, yet his work remains a prime source for the Viking Age. The book endures as a vast, gripping history of kings, battles, and faith in the North.
6002-little-miss-by-the-day:
Lucille Van Slyke chases an elusive figure she calls little Miss By-the-Day, a whimsical young person who slips out of towns, countries, and even rooms just before one arrives. The narrator feels cheated of something rightfully hers, as if a fascinating soul known perfectly well can never quite be met.

At first Miss By-the-Day sounds casual and commonplace, just a little seamstress, and the narrator lets her slip through her fingers. Chapters on a barred garden, a house in the woods, lost dreams, an unfinished song, and certain legal matters follow. Van Slyke turns a search for one girl into a meditation on near meetings.
6601-verses-and-rhymes-by-the-way:
Nora Pembroke offers verses and rhymes made along the way, with a nod to poor Mango's poems and to Burns on the lowly daisy. Her dedication speaks to a dear friend who stood near in dark days, and thanks a higher guide for a debt of love. The contents list a tale of Plantagenet, a legend of a Buckingham village, and poems on Ottawa and the lake.

Pembroke's verse is plain, pious, and home-like, with a taste for local names and quiet feeling. She writes for friends and neighbors, not for fame, and her rhymes carry that modest aim. Verses and Rhymes by the Way is a small, sincere book of Canadian verse from a life lived close to home.
6627-barriers-burned-away:
E. P. Roe wrote his first novel in sympathy with Chicago after its great fire, hoping its losses and fortitude might teach lessons once the news had died away. Flames, he says, can show with harsh light the need and worth of Christian faith. The book is dedicated to his mother's memory, and its preface speaks with plain, earnest feeling.

The story that follows turns on love, loss, and faith tested by fire and by the rebuilding of lives. Roe writes as a preacher-novelist, warm and direct, for readers who like a moral tale. Barriers Burned Away is a sincere, period romance of a city burned and a people remade.
6785-wallenstein-s-camp-a-play:
Schiller's Camp of Wallenstein, in James Churchill's translation, serves as an introduction to the great Wallenstein tragedy. Its vivid portrait of the general's army, the translator notes, gives the best clue to the spell of his gigantic power. Blind faith in his arms, belief in supernatural aid, wild indulgence, and scorn for all law save the camp's have swollen his soldiers with a sense of endless sway.

Oppression of peasants and plunder of the country feed that swagger, yet the camp speaks for itself in the play. A prologue passage on Schiller's view of the Camp closes the note. Wallenstein's Camp is a lively, rough prelude to one of Schiller's greatest dramas.
6790-demetrius-a-play:
Schiller's Demetrius opens at the Diet of Cracow, with the Polish senate hall in full view. On a raised platform under a canopy sits the king on his throne. Escutcheons of Poland and Lithuania hang at his sides. Ten royal officers stand by him. Bishops, palatines, and castellans sit below, and deputies stand in double line, all armed. The Archbishop of Gnesen, primate of the kingdom, sits near the front with a chaplain bearing a golden cross.

His opening speech hails a tempestuous Diet brought to a cordial close, with king and commons parting as friends. Into that calm steps a claimant who will shake the realm. Demetrius is a grand, unfinished drama of false princes and real power.
718-tono-bungay:
H. G. Wells wrote this novel about George Ponderevo, a young man drawn into the rise of his uncle Edward, a salesman of genius. Edward builds a fortune on Tono-Bungay, a patent tonic of little worth, sold with bold ads and grand claims. George, trained in science, helps build the firm even as he doubts its wares.

The novel follows the firm from shop to empire to collapse, and George from youth to disillusion. Wells uses the quack cure to satirise English business, class, and the hunger for quick wealth. It is a big, restless book, part life story and part social critique, and one of Wells's most personal novels.
763-the-round-up-a-romance-of-arizona-no:
John Murray and Marion Mills Miller novelized Edmund Day's melodrama The Round-Up into this romance of Arizona ranch life. Cowboys, cattle, and the desert form the stage, where love, loyalty, and old wrongs clash at round-up time. The stage play's bold scenes are retold in prose, with the same broad strokes and high feeling.

The novel keeps the melodrama's pace: chases, showdowns, and reconciliations follow fast. Its heroes are plain-spoken ranch folk, its villains clear-cut. The book preserves a popular stage hit in book form, and it gives modern readers a taste of the western romance as audiences first loved it, before the screen took it over.
882-sketches-by-boz-illustrative-of-ever:
Charles Dickens, as Boz, wrote these sketches of everyday life and everyday people when he was a very young man. Published one by one, then gathered, they catch London streets, shops, omnibuses, and lodgings, with illustrations by George Cruikshank and Phiz. The people are clerks, cabmen, and shabby-genteel families.

Dickens's eye for small detail and his ear for speech already mark the future novelist. The sketches are light, funny, and often touching, and they preserve a London that was vanishing even as he wrote. The volume is the best place to meet the young Dickens, before the great novels made him famous.
a-laodicean-a-story-of-to-day:
Thomas Hardy calls his novel a story of to-day and divides it into six books named for the people who rule each stretch: George Somerset, Dare and Havill, De Stancy, and Paula. His preface treats the changing of the old order in country houses, and notes the book was finished by dictation through a five months' illness. Paula Power, a rich young heiress of no firm faith, is the Laodicean of the title.

Paula owns a castle, a telegraph, and a Baptist conscience at war with her taste for the medieval. Somerset the architect, the De Stancys, father and son, and the scheming Dare fight for her hand and fortune. Hardy sets new money and new machines against old names.
a-millionaire-of-yesterday:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens in a filthy West African trading post, where Trent and his older partner Monty wait, ragged and sick, for their chance. The two men are digging for a fortune the hard way. Years later, one of them returns to England rich, with a past that must stay buried.

Forty-two chapters follow blackmail, society drawing rooms, and a woman who knows more than she should. Oppenheim, a master of the popular thriller of his day, keeps secrets stacked on secrets and pays them off in turns. The tale moves between the fever coast and London polish, and its smooth plotting carried his name around the world.
a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-botany-:
Watkin Tench, an officer of marines, offers his little tract to the public, as his introduction says, to amuse and inform about the expedition to Botany Bay. He sailed with the fleet sent to found a colony in New South Wales, a scheme some foresaw as beneficial and others called big with folly and ruin. Tench declines to judge before the trial is fair.

Fourteen chapters cover the voyage out, the landings, and the first state of the settlement at Sydney Cove. He describes the country, the convicts and officers, and the Aboriginal people with a clear, humane eye. His narrative was among the first books of Australia, and it stays fresh for its plain good sense.
a-terrible-temptation-a-story-of-to-day:
A Terrible Temptation, subtitled A Story of To-Day, is an 1871 novel by Charles Reade. Reade was a leading Victorian novelist, famous for turning close research into dramatic stories of modern life. The subtitle is his signal: unlike his historical romances, this tale is set in the England of his own day, among its present manners and pressures.

As the title promises, the story turns on a temptation and the damage it threatens to those who face it. Reade builds his fiction on strong situations and moral stakes, and this novel applies that method to contemporary society. It stands in his output as his pointed look at the temptations of modern life, written for the readers who were living it.
a-wasted-day:
Richard Harding Davis opens in the office of Arnold Thorndike, called the wisest man in Wall Street. A letter arrives from a probation officer about Spear, a young stenographer who once took Thorndike's letters on the train. Spear has been convicted of theft and faces sentence on Tuesday.

Learning what Thorndike does with that letter fills the rest of the tale. Davis contrasts the great man's busy, guarded day with the one errand that might save a foolish young clerk. The story is slight in plot but warm in feeling, and it questions what a successful man's time is really for. Davis writes the office scenes with a reporter's quick eye.
barriers-burned-away:
Edward Payson Roe's Barriers Burned Away is a novel prompted by the great Chicago fire, which Roe visited among its smouldering ruins. Roe says the sufferers' losses and fortitude taught lessons that deserved to outlast the newspaper echoes, and that even destructive flames could throw Christian faith into sharper light.

The fire itself fills only a small share of the story; the wider story follows its characters through love, pride and the social barriers that burn away under trial. Roe, dedicating the book to his mother's memory, calls it the first child of his imagination, and its early copyright dates run from 1872. Readers of sentimental Victorian fiction will find here a Chicago novel where disaster tests, rather than merely destroys, its people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-saints-da:
All Saints' Day, a solemnity on 1 November, honours all the saints, known and unknown, and, in Urban IV's words, supplies deficiencies in the year's celebration of saints' feasts. Its vigil is popularly called Hallowe'en. In the early Church Christians marked the anniversary of a martyr's death at the place of martyrdom. As martyrs multiplied under Diocletian, a separate day for each became impossible, so the Church appointed one common day.

The first trace appears at Antioch on the Sunday after Pentecost. It appears in St. Ephrem the Syrian's sermon in 373 and St. John Chrysostom's seventy-fourth homily in 407. At first the feast honoured only martyrs and St. John the Baptist, though the Chaldean Calendar already lists confessors in 411. In the West, Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon to the Virgin and all the martyrs in 609 or 610. Gregory III fixed the anniversary for 1 November, and Gregory IV extended it Church-wide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-souls-day:
All Souls' Day, the commemoration of the faithful departed, falls on 2 November, or on 3 November if the second is a Sunday or a solemnity. The clergy recite the Office of the Dead, and all Masses are Requiem Masses. Its basis is the doctrine that souls not perfectly cleansed, or not fully atoned, are barred from the Beatific Vision. The faithful on earth can aid them with prayers, alms, and especially the Mass.

Early Christians entered the departed's names in the diptychs. By the sixth century Benedictine monasteries commemorated their dead at Whitsuntide. Spain kept such a day before Sexagesima or Pentecost in Isidore's time. Germany, Widukind of Corvey testifies, prayed for the dead on 1 October. St. Odilo of Cluny ordered the annual commemoration in his monasteries, whence it spread among Benedictines and Carthusians. Liège adopted it first, under Bishop Notger. Otricus introduced it into Milan for 15 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Bergen covered the provinces Nordre and Sondre Bergenhus and Sondmor in Romsdal. The discovery at Selo in 996 of the remains of Saint Sunniva and her companions moved King Olaf Trygveson to build a church. Only in 1068 did King Olaf Kyrre found a bishopric and monastery at Selo. Bernard the Saxon served as first bishop. He later moved to the city of Bergen and died as first bishop about 1090.

In 1152 Bergen became suffragan to the metropolitan see of Trondhjem, with a cathedral chapter. Bishop Paul, from 1156 to 1194, saw Christ Church Cathedral finished. It hosted a provincial council and the coronation of King Magnus Erlingson in 1164, the first coronation of a Norwegian king. Sunniva's relics moved to the cathedral in 1170. In 1247 Cardinal Wilhelm of Sabina crowned King Haakon Haakonsson under Bishop Arne. King Magnus built a royal chapel between 1275 and 1302 to house a relic of the Crown of Thorns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ash-wednesday:
Ash Wednesday, the Wednesday after Quinquagesima Sunday, opens the Lenten fast. Its Latin name, dies cinerum, day of ashes, found in the Roman Missal and in the earliest copies of the Gregorian Sacramentary, probably dates from the eighth century at least. On that day, by ancient custom, all the faithful are urged to approach the altar before Mass begins. There the priest, dipping his thumb in blessed ashes, marks each forehead, or for clerics the tonsure place, with the cross.

He says the words, Remember, man, that thou art dust and unto dust thou shalt return. The ashes come from burning palms blessed on the previous year's Palm Sunday. Four ancient prayers bless them, they are sprinkled with holy water and scented with incense, and the celebrant himself, bishop or cardinal, receives ashes in turn. The entry explains a rite that opens Lent with dust.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bombay:
Bombay's archdiocese stretches from Bombay Island and Salsette far north to Quetta, though 200 miles of Damaun diocese cut it from its center. About 18,000 Catholics live under the archbishop, served by German Jesuits, native secular priests, and sisters teaching and doing charitable work across 24 churches and 25 chapels.

Portuguese settlers and Franciscans planted the island's churches from 1534, and the work continued after England took Bombay in 1665. Goanese clergy were expelled in 1720, and a double jurisdiction dispute, the Goan schism, long troubled the mission. Carmelites held the vicariate until 1854, Capuchins briefly followed, and by 1858 the whole Bombay-Poona mission lay with the German Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-branch-sunday: Branch Sunday was a medieval English name for Palm Sunday, born from the shortage of palms for its rites. English churches used boughs of yew, willow, or other home-grown trees, and the day took their names, as Yew Sunday, or the general term Branch Sunday. The custom shows how a feast kept its shape while local trees stood in for palms from far away.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cantate-sunda:
Cantate Sunday is the name for the fourth Sunday after Easter. It comes from the first words of the Mass introit that day, Cantate Domino novum canticum, meaning sing to the Lord a new song. Like Gaudete and Laetare Sundays in Advent and Lent, the name comes from the chant that opens the liturgy.

Names of this kind probably date from the twelfth century and were common in the Middle Ages. They were used to mark dates in everyday business as well as in church life. John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres, who died in 1182, counts among the earliest writers known to use the name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesar-egasse-:
César-Egasse du Boulay, known as Bulæus, was a French historian born early in the seventeenth century at Saint-Ellier in Mayenne and dying on 16 October 1678. After teaching humanities at the College of Navarre he rose to high posts in the University of Paris, serving as its rector and historian.

His main work, the Historia Universitatis Parisiensis, runs from the university's supposed foundation by Charlemagne in 800 down to 1600. The university censured its first three volumes, published in 1665. The king's censors, however, found nothing blameworthy, and the last three volumes appeared in 1673. The history matters for its many original documents, though its value suffers from the author's weak judgment and criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyprien-tangu:
A life sketch follows Cyprien Tanguay, a priest of Quebec born in 1819 and dead in 1902, who became the great keeper of French Canadian family records. Ordained in 1843, he spent twenty-two years in parish work, notably at Rimouski, where he helped found the future diocesan seminary. His love of family history flowered after his 1867 post with the Dominion Statistics Department.

He then spent his life gathering parish and church records across Quebec, the Maritimes, Ontario, and old French towns in the United States, visiting France twice for the same task. His great book of French Canadian families, issued from 1871 to 1890 in seven huge volumes, lets every French Canadian trace forebears to old France. Flawed in places, it stays highly reliable and nearly unique, and Leo XIII gave him a prelature in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-murray:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Murray, Archbishop of Dublin, born near Arklow in 1768. Schooled at home and at Salamanca, he was ordained in 1790 and served as curate in Dublin and Arklow. In 1798 soldiers shot his parish priest in bed, and Murray fled to Dublin to escape the same fate.

Made coadjutor bishop in 1809 at Archbishop Troy's request, he succeeded to Dublin in 1823, after a year as president of Maynooth College. An uncompromising foe of the veto and a firm backer of the Catholic Association, he backed Stanley's national education scheme and tolerated the Queen's Colleges, against Archbishop MacHale. He declined a Privy Council seat and died respected even by opponents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-jamay:
A life of Denis Jamay, a Franciscan Recollect who led the first missionary band to Canada. Chosen as provincial commissary in 1615, he sailed with Champlain, reached Tadoussac in May, and met native peoples at Sault Saint Louis. On 24 June 1615, at Rivière des Prairies, he said the first Mass of the new mission.

He sailed home in 1616 to press the colony's needs before the king and the Rouen Associates. Chosen commissary again in 1620, he returned with Champlain, urged Quebec settlers to obey the viceroy, and blessed the first regular Recollect convent, dedicated to Our Lady of the Angels. He went back to France in 1621 and died there in 1625.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-du-coudray:
Du Coudray was a French soldier born at Reims on 8 September 1738 who died at Philadelphia on 11 September 1777. Trained for the army, he shone as an engineer and served as adjutant-general of artillery, counted among the best military experts of France. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how in 1776 he volunteered to aid the American colonists against England. Silas Deane and Benjamin Franklin promised him a major-general's commission with command of the artillery.

That promise angered officers already in the army when he landed in May 1777 with twenty-nine officers and twelve artillery sergeants. Several threatened to resign, so a compromise made him inspector-general in August with major-general's rank. His grave is now unknown, the entry notes, closing a short American career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-and-jo:
Edmund Hay was a Scottish Jesuit and envoy to Mary Queen of Scots, born about 1540 and dead at Rome in 1591. In 1562 he went with Father Nicolas de Gouda on a mission from Pope Pius IV to Mary. Mary was then newly back in Scotland. Hay acted as go-between at their secret meeting at Holyrood. He also led a band of young Scots back to join the Society.

After study at Rome he served as confessor to the archduchesses at Innsbruck and later as rector of Clermont College in Paris, reporting to Rome on Scotland and its queen. The entry pairs him with his kinsman John Hay, a noted scholar and teacher who died at Pont-a-Mousson in 1608. Together they show Scots Catholics working from exile for a queen and a church under siege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-har:
The Harlay were a French family of parliamentarians and bishops. Achille de Harlay, born in 1536, became first president of the Parlement of Paris. He stood against the League and endured imprisonment in the Bastille. His long career spanned the Wars of Religion and their troubled aftermath.

Achille de Sancy, born in 1581, served as ambassador to Constantinople. He later became an Oratorian and bishop of St-Malo in 1631. Scholars in 1904 named him editor of Richelieu's Memoires. Francois de Harlay, archbishop of Rouen, reformed the abbey of Jumieges and founded an academy at Gaillon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-lecl:
Francois Leclerc du Tremblay, better known as Pere Joseph, was born at Paris on 4 November 1577 and died at Rueil on 18 December 1638. He was a Capuchin friar who became Cardinal Richelieu's grey eminence. Through his kinsman the Constable de Montmorency he appeared at court at eighteen as Baron de Maffliers and served in Henry IV's armies against Spain. On 2 February 1599 he became a Capuchin novice and was provincial of Touraine in 1613. In 1616 he helped negotiate Loudun between Marie de Medicis and Conde's malcontents, giving Richelieu his first conference with Conde.

 As Richelieu's confidant he built French Capuchin missions in the East, ten by 1633, sending missionaries to Egypt, Abyssinia, and Morocco, though the last two ventures failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galloway:
Galloway, a diocese in southwest Scotland, claims the oldest church foundation in the country. It spans Dumfries, Kirkcudbright, Wigtown, and most of Ayr, some 3,347 square miles, with 373,670 people of whom Catholics form a small share. Its founder, Saint Ninian, a Briton schooled at Rome, set his see at Whithorn in 397 and named his church for Saint Martin of Tours.

Bede calls it Candida Casa, the White House, for its unusual stone build. The bishop list broke three times for about three hundred years each, and after the last Catholic bishop died in 1558 the see lay empty for 320 years. Leo XIII restored it in 1878 under John McLachlan, who swiftly gave the scattered, mostly laboring Catholics churches, schools, presbyteries, and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaudete-sunda:
Gaudete Sunday, the third Sunday of Advent, takes its name from the Mass Introit's first word, Rejoice. Advent began as a forty-day fast after Saint Martin's feast, called Saint Martin's Lent, then shrank to four weeks by the ninth century and softened from fast to abstinence by the twelfth. Gregory the Great first ordered its Office, and Rome's Gregorian book gave Masses for its Sundays.

Like Mid-Lent's Laetare Sunday, Gaudete breaks a penitential season midway with signs of joy. Organ and flowers return, rose vestments replace purple, deacon and subdeacon resume dalmatic and tunicle, and cardinals wear rose. Its station falls at the Vatican basilica, and a new Invitatory hails not the Lord who is to come but the Lord now nigh at hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-day:
George Day, Bishop of Chichester, held the Catholic line through Henry, Edward, and Mary. Born in Shropshire about 1501 and graduated at Cambridge, he became Master of Saint John's in 1537 and provost of King's College in 1538. Consecrated bishop in 1543 by Cranmer, he defended altar doctrine in the Lords and voted against communion under both kinds and the new Prayer Book.

Day's preaching so stirred his diocese that in 1550 the Council sent Cox to counter it, then hauled Day in for refusing to tear down altars. He answered that he would rather suffer bodily than corrupt his soul, and for that contempt he sat in the Fleet and lost his see in 1551. Mary restored him at once as bishop and almoner, and Cardinal Pole confirmed him in 1555. He died in August 1556.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-hay:
George Hay, a Scottish bishop and writer born at Edinburgh in 1729, led the Lowland Catholics for nearly forty years. Bound for medicine, he tended the wounded after Prestonpans at sixteen, followed Charles Edward's army, and, after Culloden, spent twelve months in London custody. There a Catholic bookseller opened the faith to him, and he was received in December 1749.

Barred by penal laws from a medical degree, Hay took ship as a surgeon, met Bishop Challoner in London, and instead studied eight years at Rome's Scots College. Ordained in 1758, he became coadjutor in 1769 and bore the vicariate's whole burden. He printed Scotland's first English Catholic Bible and his Sincere, Devout, and Pious Christian of 1781 to 1786, still a standard work. He died in 1811.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-pray:
George Pray, an abbot, canon, and librarian born in 1723, wrote Hungary's early history from its sources. His Tyrolese family settled him at Pozsony, and he entered the Society of Jesus in 1745, studying at Vienna and Nagy-Szombat. Ordained in 1754, he taught across Hungary and at Vienna's Theresianum, tutoring the Salm princesses and lecturing on political science and moral theology.

At the Jesuits' suppression in 1773, Maria Theresa made Pray imperial historiographer at four hundred florins a year. He ran Buda's university library from 1777, surrendering his manuscripts and documents to it in 1784 for a life annuity. He became canon of Grosswardein in 1790 and abbot of Tormowa. Pray first drew notice to Hungary's oldest coherent text, the Funeral Oration of about 1199, called the Pray Codex after him. His Annals of Hungarian kings fill five volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good-friday:
Good Friday is the day in Holy Week on which the Church keeps the anniversary of the Crucifixion of Jesus Christ. In the Roman Missal it is called Feria VI in Parasceve, in the Greek liturgy the Holy and Great Friday, and in German Charfreitag, Sorrowful Friday. It is one of the two oldest feasts in the calendar. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls its office the most peculiar, composite, and dramatic in the liturgy.

Parasceve, meaning preparation, first named the sixth day's preparation for the Sabbath. By metonymy it then named the day itself. Irenaeus and Tertullian called the day the Pasch, though later writers distinguished the Pascha of death from the Pascha of resurrection. The origin of Good is unclear: some derive it from God's Friday, others from the German Gute Freitag, and the Anglo-Saxons sometimes called it Long Friday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-saturday:
Holy Saturday, once called Great Saturday, the Angelic Night, and the Vigil of Easter, closes Lent and opens paschal time. It is no longer a day of pure joy like Maundy Thursday, but one where joy and sadness mix. By a notable exception, the early church allowed fasting on this Saturday alone, and the fast was severe: from Irenaeus onward, an absolute fast held for the forty hours before Easter.

The Easter vigil itself shifted strangely over time. In the first six or seven centuries ceremonies ran through the whole night, so the Alleluia met the dawn of Resurrection day. In the eighth century they moved to Saturday afternoon, and later, by a singular anachronism, to Saturday morning. The entry follows those changes in hours, fasting, and rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-martiana:
Jean Martianay, a French Maurist Benedictine born in 1647 at Saint-Sever and dead in Paris in 1717, gave his life to the Bible. His order's annals praise his Greek and Hebrew learning. He spent over thirty years searching French libraries, above all for Jerome's works.

Martianay begged every Benedictine abbey to aid a full critical edition of Jerome, and, save for the Hieronymian Vulgate done with Pouget, he finished the vast task alone. He taught Scripture at Arles, Bordeaux, and Carcassonne. He wrote on inspiration against Richard Simon, defended the Hebrew text and Vulgate chronology, and treated the canon's history and French Bible versions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-barclay:
John Barclay was a Latin novelist and satirist whose Argenis became one of the most read political novels of its age. Born at Pont-a-Mousson in 1582, son of the jurist William Barclay, he was schooled by the Jesuits and published a commentary on Statius at nineteen. He tried his fortune in London under James I, published his Satyricon in Paris, and wrote poems and an account of the Gunpowder Plot.

His 1609 edition of his father's work denying the pope's temporal power over princes drew Bellarmine and others into a long controversy, sharpened by his 1611 Apology attacking the Jesuits. Invited to Rome by Paul V in 1616, he was pensioned by the pope, published a plea to sectaries in 1617, and finished Argenis in July 1621, dying the next month. Contemporaries admired his honesty and rare courtesy, and his friend Thorie wrote his elegy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-o-kane-m:
John O'Kane Murray was an Irish-American physician and popular historian of American Catholicism. Born in County Antrim in 1847, he came with his parents to New York in 1856 and studied at Saint John's College, Fordham. He took his medical degree in New York and practiced in Brooklyn until 1880. He spent his last five years fighting the tuberculosis that killed him at Chicago in 1885.

A constant contributor to the Catholic press, he compiled books that found wide readership and always exerted a good influence. They were a Popular History of the Catholic Church in the United States in 1876 and Poets and Poetry of Ireland in 1877. The list continues with Catholic Heroes and Heroines in 1878, Little Lives of Great Saints in 1879, Catholic Pioneers of America in 1881, and Lessons in English Literature in 1883. He also revised Kearney's General History and had begun the same work on Lingard's England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jubilate-sund:
Jubilate Sunday is the third Sunday after Easter in the Catholic liturgy. Its name comes from the first word of the Mass Introit, Jubilate Deo omnis terra, shout joyfully to God, all the earth, from Psalm 65. With the two Sundays that follow, it carries on the Church's song of joy in the Resurrection through Paschaltide.

During Eastertide, Alleluia joins every antiphon, responsory, and versicle of Office and Mass. The Jubilate Introit invites all to joy. The Epistle urges the faithful, above all penitents and the newly baptized, to obey lawful powers and live as worthy disciples of the risen Christ. The Gospel counsels patience under life's trials for the sake of heaven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judica-sunday:
Judica Sunday is the fifth Sunday of Lent, better known as Passion Sunday. Its name comes from the Introit's opening words, Judica me, Deus, judge me, O God, from Psalm 42. In Germany it is called Black Sunday from the veiling of crosses and statues, once done at the Gospel words Jesus hid himself.

On this day the Judica psalm drops from the start of Mass until Easter, and the Gloria is omitted to mark the shame of Christ's Passion, when his glory seemed laid aside. The whole Office and Mass turn solemn, preparing for Holy Week. Rome once kept the day's station at the Vatican Basilica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laetare-sunda:
Laetare Sunday, the fourth or middle Sunday of Lent, takes its name from the Mass introit Laetare Jerusalem, Rejoice, O Jerusalem. Early Lent began after Quinquagesima with only thirty-six fast days, until four days were added to make forty.

Strictly the Thursday before is Lent's midpoint, once marked as such, but signs of joy meant to hearten penitents moved to the Sunday. Flowers deck the altar, the organ sounds at Mass and Vespers, rose vestments replace purple, and deacon and subdeacon wear dalmatics rather than folded chasubles. Rome's station stood at St. Croce in Gerusalemme, the Golden Rose was blessed then, and the day also passed as Refreshment Sunday, Mid-Lent, and Mothering Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lettice-mary-:
Lettice Mary Tredway, called Lady Tredway (1595-1677), was Sir Walter Tredway's daughter. In July 1616 she entered the novitiate at Sin, near Douai, of the Lateran Canonesses Regular of Notre-Dame-de-Beaulieu. In October 1617 she made solemn profession. In 1631 she and Father Carre planned a house for English canonesses only at Douai.

 In 1634 it was settled to open this English convent at Paris, with Dr. Smith, Bishop of Chalcedon, exiled in Paris, helped so generously he counts as co-founder. He blessed her as abbess, and Notre-Dame-de-Sion was firmly set up in the Rue des Fosses in 1639. They also practically founded the Seminary of St. Gregory for the English Mission.  She stayed abbess till 1675, when infirmity forced her to resign.  For forty-one years she laboured bravely for her convent, and the community, forced to leave France, now stands at Ealing in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-low-sunday:
Low Sunday is the first Sunday after Easter, named, it seems, for its contrast with the great feast just past. As the octave day of Easter it still belongs to that feast, though in a lower degree.

Its liturgical name, Dominica in albis depositis, recalls the newly baptized, who on this day first laid aside their white robes, a custom Augustine already mentions. Writers also call it Pascha clausum, the close of Easter week, and Quasimodo Sunday, from its Mass introit, Quasi modo geniti infantes, a name still common in France and Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludger-duvern:
Ludger Duvernay was a French-Canadian journalist and patriot, born at Vercheres in 1799 and dead in 1852. A printer by trade, he founded papers at Three Rivers and Quebec, then La Minerve at Montreal in 1827 with Morin, a leading voice of French Canada.

Jailed in 1832 for protesting the Legislative Council with Tracey, he won a medal for public devotion. His lasting deed was founding the Society of St. John the Baptist in 1834, choosing the Precursor as patron, the maple leaf as emblem, and the motto Our language, our institutions, and our laws. Exiled for the 1837 rebellions, he returned to revive La Minerve under responsible government.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-cosway:
Maria Cosway was a miniature painter, born at Florence in 1759 and dead at Lodi in 1838. Her maiden name was Hadfield, her father an Englishman. She drew with great talent young, and at nineteen joined Florence's Academy of Fine Arts, where Visitation nuns had schooled her. Her father died in 1778, and Angelica Kauffman brought her to England.

There she married Richard Cosway, a leading miniature painter, in London in 1781. She showed at the Academy until 1801, though her mythological oils won less praise than her miniatures and copies of her husband's work. Her London Sunday concerts drew notice from Horace Walpole. At Cardinal Fesch's urging she opened a girls' school at Lyons, closed by war in 1811, then founded one at Lodi in 1812. She bought its buildings, joined its community to the Dames Inglesi, and gave her life and fortune to the school. Emperor Francis I made her a baroness in 1834.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maundy-thursd:
Maundy Thursday, also called Holy Thursday, solemnly marks the founding of the Eucharist and stands as the oldest rite peculiar to Holy Week. In early Rome the day gathered extra ceremonies: the blessing of the holy oils and the welcome back of penitents. Both were practical steps ahead of Easter, when candidates finished their preparation. The day's central Mass, the Missa chrismalis, blessed oils for the year ahead.

Custom varied by place: Rome kept everything in daylight, while Africa held the Eucharist after the evening meal to mirror the Last Supper more closely. A Carthage canon excused the faithful from fasting before Communion that day, since bathing and fasting were deemed at odds. Augustine notes that some churches offered the oblation twice, morning and evening. The entry thus opens a window on how the early Church shaped its holiest week.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melleray:
Melleray, in Brittany's Loire-Inferieure and the Diocese of Nantes near Chateaubriand, was founded about 1134. Foulques, Abbot of Pontron in Anjou, sent monks from Loroux, a daughter of Citeaux, to plant a monastery in Brittany. They loved the solitude of a spot near Old Melleray, shown by Rivallon, pastor of Auverne, and given by owner Alain de Moisdon. Guitern, first abbot, raised the monastery in 1145, but the church was finished only in 1183 under Geffroy, the fourth abbot.

Built for about twelve religious, Melleray stayed regular until wealth and commendatory abbots loosened discipline in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Etienne de Breze in 1544 was the first commendatory abbot. Decline lasted until late in the seventeenth century, when Dom Jouard restored St. Bernard's rule and the buildings. Suppressed in 1791, its few religious scattered, yet Melleray lived on through Trappists sheltered at Val Sainte in Switzerland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melo-uruguay:
Melo, a planned diocese in Uruguay, was decided in 1897 as one of two sees suffragan to Montevideo, but political causes have so far blocked all appointments. Talks to renew diplomatic ties between the Republic and the Holy See are under way. Since state recognition of the new dioceses is a condition of resumption, approval will probably come shortly. The diocese is to take in Uruguay's north-east.

Its bounds will cover, in whole or part, Cerro Largo, Rivera, Tacuarembo, and Treinta y Tres. The area runs some 19,600 square miles. Barely 145,000 people lived there in 1906, practically all Catholic. The land is very fertile, yet farming is slight, since most people, largely Brazilians, breed cattle. Melo town, founded in 1796, is Cerro Largo's capital with about 7,000 souls, near the Tacuari River some 315 miles north of Montevideo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natal-day:
A natal day, from Latin natalis and natalicium, is what we call a birthday, the anniversary of the day a man was born. Greek genesia and genethlios served the same use. In both tongues the primitive sense widened even before Christianity. Latin natalis sometimes meant little more than anniversary, and covered the emperor's accession day as well as his birthday.

Games held on an emperor's birthday in life often continued after his deification on that anniversary, as if he still lived. Greek genesia often marked the annual commemoration of a dead person by sacrifices and rites, held on his birthday rather than his death day. When Smyrna's Christians about 150 described gathering Polycarp's bones, they spoke of meeting in gladness on his natal day. From that usage grew the church's feast of a martyr's heavenly birthday, his death day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-year-s-da:
New Year's Day opens with the word year, etymologically the same as hour, signifying a going or movement, while in Semitic tongues year means repetition of the sun's course. Since the year's circle has no necessary starting point, nations and epochs chose widely different New Year dates. Spring's opening was a natural beginning, and the Bible links the year's start closely with seasons.

The ancient Roman year began in March, but Julius Caesar, correcting the calendar in 46 BC, made January the first month. Christian nations universally adopted that custom, though September through December, the seventh through tenth months, recall March's start. Christian writers and councils condemned the Saturnalia's heathen orgies at year's beginning, and Tertullian rebuked Christians treating strenae gifts as mere friendly tokens. The entry follows later customs and church observance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-norway:
Norway, the western half of the Scandinavian peninsula, rises in high plateaus cut by deep fjords along the Atlantic. Mountains like Snähätten and Galdhöppigen tower over valleys, lakes like Mjøsen spread inland, and islands offshore feed shipping and fishing, with twenty million cod a year from Lofoten alone.

Oats and barley, not wheat, make the daily bread, cattle and sheep number in the millions, and Lapps herd over a hundred thousand reindeer in the north. The entry moves from land and livelihood to church history, missions, and the Catholic life of a Lutheran kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-a:
Our Lady of Ambronay is a sanctuary of the Blessed Virgin at Ambronay in France, counted one of the two candles of devotion to Our Lady in the Diocese of Belley. Recluses founded the first church in the seventh century. Saracens destroyed it, and Saint Barnard rebuilt it about 803, together with the famed monastery of the same name.

Mid-thirteenth-century rebuilding gave the church a grander scale. It still stands, despite the ravages of 1793, as a grand diocesan landmark. Its windows, sacristy, altar, and spiral stair draw notice, and the facade of one nave dates from the ninth century. Pilgrims have long sought the shrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palm-sunday:
Palm Sunday, the sixth and last Sunday of Lent, opens Holy Week and ranks so high that no commemoration of any kind is allowed in its Mass. In common law it starts the Easter duty season. The Roman Missal sets its station at Saint John Lateran, where the pope led the rites before September 1870. Greeks keep the day with great solemnity, calling it the Sunday of the branches, or Lazarus Sunday, for Lazarus's raising the day before.

Latin books name it Sunday in Palms, or Hosanna Sunday, from the crowd's cry in the procession. Since every great feast recalled the resurrection and bore the name Pascha, it also won names like flowery Easter, and Florida took its name from this day in 1512. Blessing flowers woven among palms gave it the name Flower Sunday, known in England, Germany, and Slav lands alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraguay:
